eras.title: Western Zhou
eras.text: The Zhou overthrow the Shang and rule through a feudal network of relatives, justifying their rule by the 'Mandate of Heaven'.

eras.title: Spring and Autumn, Warring States
eras.text: Zhou authority fades and rival states compete for power. The Zhou era lays the philosophical foundations of Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism; Confucius teaches in this period.

eras.title: The Qin unification
eras.text: The First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, conquers all rivals, standardises script, coins and laws, links the northern walls and is buried with the Terracotta Army. His dynasty collapses soon after his death.

eras.title: The Han dynasty
eras.text: The Han dynasty rules for four centuries, establishes a long-lasting imperial order, makes Confucianism the state ideology and fosters advances such as papermaking. It fights the Xiongnu nomads of the steppe.

eras.title: Division
eras.text: China splits into the Three Kingdoms and then into northern dynasties ruled largely by steppe peoples and southern Chinese dynasties. Buddhism spreads widely.

eras.title: Sui and Tang
eras.text: The Sui reunify China and build the Grand Canal; the Tang make Chang'an the world's largest city, a cosmopolitan capital of poets (Li Bai, Du Fu), Buddhist monasteries and foreign merchants. The An Lushan rebellion (755) begins a long decline.

eras.title: The Song dynasty
eras.text: A commercial revolution: the Song print books with movable type, use paper money, the magnetic compass and gunpowder, and have the world's largest cities and economy. The north is lost to the Jurchen Jin (1127); the Mongols conquer the south by 1279.

eras.title: The Mongol Yuan
eras.text: Kublai Khan rules China from Khanbaliq (Beijing) as part of the Mongol world empire, open to foreigners like Marco Polo. Floods, plague and rebellion end Mongol rule.

eras.title: The Ming dynasty
eras.text: The Ming dynasty restores Chinese rule, moves the capital to Beijing and builds the Forbidden City. Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He's treasure fleets sail as far as East Africa.

eras.title: The Qing dynasty
eras.text: Manchus from the north-east conquer China and, under Kangxi and Qianlong, double its territory to include Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia and Taiwan. In the 19th century the Opium Wars and the Taiping Rebellion devastate the empire, which falls in 1911.

eras.title: The Republic of China
eras.text: Warlords divide the new republic; the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek fight the Communists and a Japanese invasion (1937–45).

eras.title: The People's Republic
eras.text: Mao Zedong's Communists win the civil war. The Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution cause catastrophe; from 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms make China the world's manufacturing centre and a superpower.

eras.title: The world's largest land empire
eras.text: Genghis Khan unites the steppe tribes and his armies conquer northern China, Central Asia, Persia and Russia. His successors invade Europe (1241) and sack Baghdad (1258). The 'Pax Mongolica' opens the Silk Road to merchants like the Polos.

eras.title: Four khanates
eras.text: The empire splits into the Yuan in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia and the Golden Horde in Russia.

eras.title: Mongol Central Asia
eras.text: Genghis Khan's son Chagatai inherits Central Asia; the khanate controls the heart of the Silk Road between China and Persia.

eras.title: Moghulistan
eras.text: In the 1340s the khanate splits into western and eastern halves. Timur annexes the west in 1363, while the east survives as Moghulistan.

eras.title: The first steppe empire
eras.text: Under Modu Chanyu the Xiongnu nomads create a vast confederation on the Mongolian steppe that extracts tribute from Han China until Han campaigns split them.

eras.title: India's first great empire
eras.text: Chandragupta Maurya, advised by Chanakya, unites northern India; his grandson Ashoka conquers Kalinga, converts to Buddhism and spreads his edicts of compassion across the subcontinent.

eras.title: The classical age of India
eras.text: The Guptas rule northern India in an era of peace and prosperity: Aryabhata's astronomy, the decimal system with zero, Kalidasa's poetry and the Ajanta cave paintings. Hunnic invasions break the empire.

eras.title: Crossroads of the Silk Road
eras.text: Kushans from Central Asia rule from Afghanistan to the Ganges, trading with Rome, Parthia and Han China. Under Kanishka, Gandharan art blends Greek and Buddhist styles and Buddhism spreads to China.

eras.title: Early Cholas
eras.text: An ancient Tamil dynasty of south India, mentioned in Ashoka's edicts and Tamil Sangam poetry.

eras.title: The imperial Cholas
eras.text: Rajaraja I and Rajendra I build a maritime empire across south India and Sri Lanka, raid Srivijaya, and build the great temple at Thanjavur. Their bronzes are among the masterpieces of Indian art.

eras.title: Turkic sultans in India
eras.text: Turkic and Afghan dynasties rule northern India from Delhi, fend off the Mongols and build the Qutb Minar. Under Muhammad bin Tughluq the sultanate briefly covers most of India.

eras.title: After Timur
eras.text: Timur's sack of Delhi (1398) shatters the sultanate; the Lodi dynasty rules a smaller state until Babur defeats it at Panipat in 1526.

eras.title: The City of Victory
eras.text: A Hindu empire in south India whose capital at Hampi amazed Portuguese and Persian visitors. It thrives on the spice and horse trade until defeated by the Deccan sultanates at Talikota (1565).

eras.title: Babur to Akbar
eras.text: Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founds the empire. His grandson Akbar conquers most of northern India, builds an efficient administration and encourages tolerance among faiths.

eras.title: Splendour
eras.text: Under Jahangir, Shah Jahan (builder of the Taj Mahal) and Aurangzeb, the empire reaches its greatest extent under Aurangzeb. Mughal India produces about a quarter of the world's manufacturing output.

eras.title: Decline
eras.text: After Aurangzeb, the Marathas, Persians, Afghans and the British East India Company carve up the empire; the last emperor is exiled after the 1857 rebellion.

eras.title: The Marathas
eras.text: Shivaji founds a Hindu kingdom in the western Deccan; the Maratha Confederacy becomes the dominant power in India in the 18th century, until defeated by the British.

eras.title: Company rule
eras.text: After Plassey (1757) the British East India Company conquers India piece by piece, ruling through its own army and puppet princes.

eras.title: The British Raj
eras.text: After the 1857 rebellion the Crown takes direct rule; railways are built and famines recur. Gandhi's and Nehru's Congress leads a mass independence movement.

eras.title: Independent India
eras.text: India becomes independent amid Partition and develops into the world's largest democracy and, by 2023, its most populous country.

eras.title: Pakistan
eras.text: Created as a homeland for South Asia's Muslims at Partition; East Pakistan breaks away as Bangladesh in 1971. Military and civilian governments alternate.

eras.title: The empire of Angkor
eras.text: Khmer god-kings rule much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, a vast city with sophisticated reservoirs, where they build Angkor Wat and the Bayon. Siamese attacks lead to Angkor's abandonment in 1431.

eras.title: Lords of the straits
eras.text: A Buddhist maritime empire based at Palembang on Sumatra controls the Strait of Malacca — the sea route between India and China — and is a centre of Buddhist learning.

eras.title: The temples of Bagan
eras.text: The first kingdom to unify Burma builds over 10,000 Buddhist temples on the plain of Bagan; it declines after Mongol invasions.

eras.title: Sukhothai
eras.text: The first Thai kingdom; King Ram Khamhaeng is credited with creating the Thai script.

eras.title: Ayutthaya
eras.text: Ayutthaya grows into a great trading city of Southeast Asia, welcoming Chinese, Japanese, Persian and European merchants, until the Burmese sack it in 1767.

eras.title: Bangkok and the Chakri dynasty
eras.text: The Chakri kings rule from Bangkok; Siam (Thailand) is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by Europeans.

eras.title: Đại Việt
eras.text: After a thousand years of Chinese rule, the Vietnamese win independence (938). Dynasties such as the Lý, Trần and Lê repel the Mongols three times and expand south at the expense of Champa.

eras.title: French Indochina
eras.text: France conquers Vietnam step by step; Ho Chi Minh leads the independence struggle that defeats the French at Dien Bien Phu (1954).

eras.title: War and reunification
eras.text: Vietnam is divided, then reunified under communist rule after the Vietnam War. After an economic crisis, the Đổi Mới reforms begin in 1986.

eras.title: Champa
eras.text: Hindu and later Muslim Cham kingdoms along the central Vietnamese coast grow rich on maritime trade, rival Angkor and Đại Việt, and are gradually absorbed by Vietnam.

eras.title: Asuka and Nara
eras.text: Buddhism and Chinese-style government reach Japan from Korea and China. After defeat by Tang China at the Battle of Baekgang, Japan's rulers build a more centralised state on Chinese models.

eras.title: The Heian period
eras.text: An elegant court culture flourishes in Kyoto, dominated by the Fujiwara clan; Lady Murasaki writes 'The Tale of Genji'. Samurai clans grow powerful in the provinces.

eras.title: Kamakura and Muromachi shogunates
eras.text: Military rulers (shoguns) govern in the emperor's name. Japan repels two Mongol invasions (1274, 1281); Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony develop.

eras.title: The Warring States
eras.text: Japan fractures into feuding domains. Portuguese traders bring guns (1543) and missionaries; Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi reunify the country.

eras.title: Tokugawa Japan
eras.text: The Tokugawa shoguns keep two and a half centuries of peace and largely close Japan to foreigners; Edo (Tokyo) becomes one of the world's largest cities.

eras.title: Imperial Japan
eras.text: The Meiji Restoration modernises Japan at breakneck speed. It defeats China (1895) and Russia (1905), annexes Korea and invades China, then attacks the US; it surrenders in 1945.

eras.title: Postwar Japan
eras.text: Under a new pacifist constitution, Japan recovers from the war and enjoys decades of rapid growth, the 'Japanese economic miracle'.

eras.title: The Three Kingdoms
eras.text: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla compete for the peninsula, absorbing Buddhism and Chinese culture and passing them on to Japan.

eras.title: Unified Silla
eras.text: Silla, allied with Tang China, unites most of the peninsula; its capital Gyeongju is a centre of Buddhist art.

eras.title: Goryeo
eras.text: The Goryeo dynasty, which gives Korea its name, rules the peninsula and endures decades of Mongol domination, until it is overthrown in 1392.

eras.title: Joseon
eras.text: General Yi Seong-gye founds the Confucian Joseon dynasty, which lasts until 1897. King Sejong the Great creates the Hangul alphabet, and Admiral Yi Sun-sin helps defeat the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598.

eras.title: Colony and division
eras.text: Japan annexes Korea (1910–45). After liberation, it is divided into a communist North and a capitalist South, which fight the Korean War (1950–53).

eras.title: The Tibetan Empire
eras.text: Songtsen Gampo unites Tibet in the 7th century. At its height the Tibetan Empire rivals Tang China, and Buddhism is introduced from India and China.

eras.title: Lamas and lords
eras.text: After the empire breaks up, Buddhist monastic orders grow powerful; the Sakya lamas govern Tibet under Mongol protection.

eras.title: The Dalai Lamas
eras.text: The Fifth Dalai Lama becomes ruler of Tibet and builds the Potala Palace; Tibet comes under Qing overlordship, then is de facto independent from 1913 until China takes control in 1950.

eras.title: The Uyghur Khaganate
eras.text: A Turkic steppe empire allied with Tang China, which it helps save during the An Lushan rebellion; its rulers adopt Manichaeism.

eras.title: The Turkic Khaganate
eras.text: Under Bumin Qaghan and his sons, the Göktürks overthrow the Rouran and found the First Turkic Khaganate, a nomadic empire across Inner Asia.

eras.title: The Khazar Khaganate
eras.text: A Turkic trading empire between the Black Sea and Caspian whose elite famously converts to Judaism; it controls the route between the Islamic world, Byzantium and the Rus'.

eras.title: Dutch East Indies
eras.text: The Dutch East India Company and then the Netherlands gradually conquer the archipelago, drawn by its spices.

eras.title: Indonesia
eras.text: Sukarno declares independence in 1945; after a war with the Dutch it becomes the world's largest Muslim-majority country.

eras.title: Afghanistan
eras.text: Founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, Afghanistan becomes a buffer state in the Great Game between British India and the Russian Empire. Since 1978 it has suffered decades of war, including the Soviet war of 1979–1989 and the US-led war from 2001 to 2021.
